def: The standard deviation of an estimate across repeated samples, such as sigma divided by the square root of n for a mean.
A range computed from data by a method that contains the true value in a stated share (such as 95%) of repeated experiments.
A confidence interval for a proportion that stays inside 0 and 1 and covers near the stated rate even for small samples and extreme rates.
Estimating how a statistic varies by recomputing it on many resamples of the data drawn with replacement.
A bootstrap that resamples whole questions so each keeps both systems' results together, giving a tighter interval for the difference.
The default claim of no real difference, whose implied chance behaviour a hypothesis test compares the data against.
The probability, if the null hypothesis were true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed; it is not the probability that the null is true.
A hypothesis test that shuffles group labels many times to build the null distribution of a statistic without any formula.

term: Type I and Type II errors
def: A Type I error is a false positive (rejecting a true null); a Type II error is a false negative (missing a real effect).
The probability that a test detects an effect of a given size when it is real; sample size scales with one over the effect squared.
The exaggeration of effect sizes among results that pass a significance filter in underpowered experiments.
Checking a running experiment repeatedly and stopping at the first significant result, which inflates the false-positive rate well above the nominal level.
Planned repeated looks at an experiment using stricter per-look boundaries so the overall false-positive rate stays at the stated level.
The accumulation of false-positive chances when many tests are run, corrected by methods such as Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg.
A split of users between experiment arms that differs from the planned ratio by more than chance allows, signalling broken assignment or logging.
